Findings.Comment: The new `/orders/{id}/lines` handler injects `JdbcTemplate` and runs `SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?` directly from the controller, bypassing `OrderService` entirely. The project guideline makes this blocking: controllers must not access the database (`JdbcTemplate`, repository) and every query must go through a service. A caller of `/orders/{id}/lines` therefore reaches order-line data without any service-layer authorization or validation, unlike `/orders/{id}` which correctly delegates to `orders.find(id)`. Move the query behind a method on `OrderService` (or a dedicated service) and have the controller call that instead.

Evidence: return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Findings.Comment: The end-index clamp was removed, so `page` now slices with `start+size` even when the last page is partial. With `items` of length 10 and `page(items, 4, 3)`, `start` is 9 (passes the `start >= len(items)` guard) but `start+size` is 12, and since the slice's capacity equals its length, `items[start : start+size]` panics with an out-of-range slice bound. Any caller paging through a list whose length is not a multiple of `size` hits this on the final page.
Findings.Headline: Last partial page panics: `page` no longer clamps the end index

Expected.why: Without the clamp, start+size passes len(items) on a partial last page and the slice expression panics. No blocking rule covers it.

Findings.Comment: `Deliver` now returns as soon as `retryable(lastErr)` is true and keeps looping only when it is false. Since `retryable` is `!errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent)`, that inverts the retry policy: a webhook answering 503 (transient status) aborts delivery after a single attempt, while a 404 or other permanent rejection is retried 5 times with backoff and then wrapped in "giving up". This is the exact opposite of the pre-change `if !retryable(err) { return err }` and of the doc comment on `Deliver` ("A transient failure is retried with exponential backoff, a permanent one is returned at once").
Findings.Headline: Retry check inverted: transient failures abort, permanent ones retried
Evidence: // Deliver posts body to ep. A transient failure is retried with exponential
// backoff, a permanent one is returned at once.

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` now ignores its `ctx` parameter entirely: the request is built and the body is read against `context.Background()` instead. A caller that cancels its context or hits a deadline — an HTTP handler whose client disconnects, a job with a timeout — can no longer abort the diff fetch, so the goroutine keeps the request and body read alive until the server responds or the connection dies. This also directly contradicts the doc comment above the function, which promises the caller's context bounds the whole operation including the body read. Both the `NewRequestWithContext` call and the `getTextCapped` call need to use `ctx`.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff drops the caller's context and cannot be cancelled
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.
func (c *Client) FetchDiff(ctx context.Context, project, repo string, pr int) (string, error) {

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` still converts the duration with `d.Seconds()` even though this change switches `Store.Touch` (and the `Redis.PExpire`/`SetPX` interface it wraps) to milliseconds. Passing a 30-second hold sends `30` to `PExpire`, which the store documents as millis, so the session TTL is set to 30ms and the session vanishes during the very export `Hold` exists to protect. Sub-second durations truncate to 0 and are rejected by `Store.Touch`'s non-positive-TTL guard despite passing the `d <= 0` check here. This bites on every `Hold` call once the store-side unit change lands.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds to a store API that now expects milliseconds
Evidence: func (s *Store) Touch(ctx context.Context, id string, ttlMillis int64) error {
return fmt.Errorf("session: touch %s: non-positive ttl %dms", id, ttlMillis)
PExpire(ctx context.Context, key string, ttlMillis int64) (existed bool, err error)

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: `Delete` reads and writes `c.items` without acquiring `c.mu`, while `Set` and `Get` both lock the mutex around every map access. When a caller invokes `Delete` concurrently with `Set` or `Get` — the normal case for a shared cache — the runtime can hit a concurrent map read/write and crash the process with a fatal `concurrent map writes` error, and the delete can also race with an in-flight `Set` to leave the map in an inconsistent state.
Findings.Headline: Cache.Delete accesses the map without holding the mutex
Findings.Suggestion:
func (c *Cache) Delete(key string) bool {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := c.items[key]
	delete(c.items, key)
	return ok
}

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `sourceAccountId` and `requesterAccountId` are both `Long`, so `!=` compares object identity, not numeric value. For any account id outside the `Long` cache range (-128..127) — practically every real account id — two boxes holding the same value are distinct objects, so the check throws `TransferAccessDeniedException` for the legitimate owner. A user with account id 500 calling `cancel(id, 500L)` on their own pending transfer is denied and the reserved funds are never released.
Findings.Headline: Long identity comparison denies the owner in cancel
Evidence: public Transfer cancel(Long transferId, Long requesterAccountId) {

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: Replacing `defer r.mu.Unlock()` with a bare `r.mu.Unlock()` at the end of the happy path means the early return for an unknown slug now exits while still holding `r.mu`. Any caller that passes a slug missing from `r.byslug` leaves the registry permanently locked, so every subsequent `Disable` call (and any other method taking `r.mu`) blocks forever on `r.mu.Lock()`. Unlock on all return paths, e.g. keep the deferred unlock and drop the explicit one.
Findings.Headline: Early return in Registry.Disable leaves the mutex locked forever

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

The prior code returned `r.Body` in exactly this case, and the comment "Ticket is optional" makes the nil path clearly intended to be supported — a body without a ticket renders, it must not crash.
Findings.Headline: Nil ticket falls through and panics in Summarize
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Findings.Comment: The end-of-window clamp now sets `last` to `len(lines)+1`, one past the end of the slice, so `lines[first:last]` at the return panics with a slice-bounds error as soon as the context window reaches the file end. Concretely: `lines` has 10 elements, `h.Start=5`, `h.Count=2`, `n=3` gives `first=7`, `last=10`; the `>=` branch fires and sets `last=11`, and `lines[7:11]` panics. This also contradicts the function's own comment that the window "must stop at the last line of the file" — the clamp now ends one line past it (and if the caller's slice has spare capacity, `lines[first:last]` silently returns garbage beyond the file instead of panicking).
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter clamps past slice end and panics at file end

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The diff drops the `q.mu.Lock()` / `q.mu.Unlock()` around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` in `worker`, but `Submit` and `Depth` still protect `depth` and `pending` with `q.mu`. When a caller submits while the worker is finishing `q.run(j)`, `len(q.pending)` reads the slice header concurrently with `Submit`'s `append` and the assignment writes `q.depth` concurrently with `Depth`'s read — a data race on the `Queue` fields. Under the Go memory model that is undefined behavior: the race detector will flag it, and `Depth()` can return a stale or torn value that misreports the backlog to whoever consumes it.
Findings.Headline: Backlog depth updated without the mutex in Queue.worker

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: `return this.refresh(base)` inside the `try` returns the promise without awaiting it, so a rejection from `provider.fetch` (or `cache.set`) is not caught by the adjacent `catch` — in an async function only `return await promise` routes a rejection through the surrounding `try/catch`. On realistic input (provider down or throwing for a base that already has an expired cached table) `getRates` rejects instead of serving the expired table, so the stale-fallback path, the `staleServed` counter and the warning log are all dead code and requests fail exactly as before this change.
Findings.Headline: Stale-fallback catch never runs: refresh promise is returned un-awaited

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `tx.Commit(ctx)`'s error is discarded, so any commit failure (serialization failure, constraint violation deferred to commit, connection drop, context cancellation) is reported to the caller as success. A caller that records a team's project claim and then proceeds will believe the claim is persisted when the row was never committed, and the deferred rollback is a no-op at that point, leaving the claim silently lost.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim swallows the commit error and reports success

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: This change inverts the error mapping the doc comment above `Owner` promises: the `errors.Is(err, errNoRows)` branch (line 20) now wraps the raw driver error, while real database faults (line 23) wrap `ErrNoClaim`. Callers matching on `ErrNoClaim` to mean "nobody owns it" will therefore treat a connection failure or query error as "project is unowned", and will fail to recognize an actually unclaimed project because `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false on the no-rows path. Any code that decides ownership (and possibly grants or denies access) off this sentinel gets the wrong answer as soon as the database misbehaves.
Findings.Headline: Owner() inverts ErrNoClaim and raw-error mapping

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
